To mitigate these threats, the review highlights four key integrative strategies: (1) adoption of ecosystemic models (e.g., A. Maleki’s Higher Education Integrity Ecosystem) linking governance, assessment, cultural norms, and individual agency; (2) implementation of process-oriented, authentic assessment frameworks (e.g., S. Lehane, A. Wright and P. Fenton’s Model for Practice and P.D.N. Ncube et al.’s PRISMA-based multi-stage evaluations) that render automated cheating obsolete; (3) operationalization of the AI3 model that integrated AI, academic integrity, and assessment innovation (C. DeLuca, L.Volante and M. Holden), and (4) proactive educational initiatives, AI literacy, and epistemic pluralism to safeguard neurodivergent learning trajectories. Ultimately, the academic community is transitioning from technocratic panic to building ethically resilient, adaptive educational ecosystems aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 4 and SDG 16).

paper_title: Barriers and Facilitators to the Implementation of Pre-Symptomatic Genetic Testing in Clinical Practice: An Updated Systematic Review
paper_abstract: Pre-symptomatic genetic and genomic testing can identify individuals at increased disease risk before symptoms emerge, but implementation depends on patient, clinician, organisational and system factors. This updated systematic review examined barriers and facilitators to implementation after the search period of Shen et al. (through 22 May 2020). PubMed was searched on 3 August 2026 using three independently constructed search sets for genetic/genomic testing, presymptomatic/asymptomatic screening, and implementation-related evidence, combined as #1 AND #2 AND #3. English-language records from 2020–2026 were screened, with publication dates audited against the update boundary. One reviewer conducted screening, eligibility assessment, design-appropriate JBI critical appraisal, extraction and narrative thematic synthesis. Of 824 records identified before filtering, 347 were screened, 91 reports were sought, 80 full texts were assessed, and 63 studies were included. Across 424 extracted barrier/facilitator findings, system-level determinants were most frequent (141 findings across 47 studies), followed by patient-level determinants (103 across 40). Thirty-four of 58 themes from Shen et al. were confirmed, while 17 additional themes were identified, including care-pathway design and follow-up, health equity and representativeness, workforce capacity, organisational readiness, logistics, and family dynamics. The post-2020 evidence places greater emphasis on operational delivery and health-system capacity, although comparisons with the earlier review are limited by PubMed-only coverage and a single-reviewer workflow. Implementation should therefore be understood as a care pathway extending beyond the genetic test itself.

paper_title: Designing Digital Courses for 21st-Century and Future Skills in Open Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
paper_abstract: Background: Higher education increasingly uses digital, blended, flipped, and open online learning to develop 21st-century skills. However, evidence on their effectiveness remains fragmented across disciplines and learning contexts. Objective: To synthesize evidence on the effects of digitally redesigned courses on 21st-century and future-oriented skills among higher- and professional-education learners.Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020. Comparative quantitative studies evaluating digital, blended, flipped, or open online course designs against traditional or alternative instruction were eligible. A second search covered studies published from 2024–2026. Study quality was assessed using an MMAT-informed approach. Random-effects meta-analyses using restricted maximum likelihood estimation were conducted in STATA 17, with Hedges’ g and 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed using I², τ², Q, and H², and publication bias using contour-enhanced funnel plots and Egger’s test. Results: Nineteen studies were included. Digital course designs showed a moderate-to-large positive effect on 21st-century skills (Hedges’ g = 0.73, 95% CI 0.68–0.78; p < 0.001), with moderate heterogeneity (τ² = 0.01; I² = 46.54%). Effects differed significantly by pedagogical approach, OER use, assessment type, and frequency of use. The largest effects were observed for constructivist-CBE hybrid approaches (g = 0.87), portfolio-based assessment (g = 0.94), and continuous use (g = 0.83). No significant differences were found by delivery format or geographic region. Funnel-plot findings suggested possible publication bias. Conclusions: Digitally redesigned courses can strengthen 21st-century skills, particularly when technology supports active, task-oriented learning and continuous assessment. More skill-specific studies outside health-professions education are needed.

paper_title: Assessment in the Age of Generative AI: Academic Integrity, Authentic Learning and Assessment Design in Tanzanian Universities — A Systematic Review
paper_abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT can now produce essays, problem solutions and examination answers that pass as competent student work, raising the question of whether university grades still show what students know and can do. This systematic review with thematic synthesis examined what the international and African literature reports on GenAI and academic integrity, the effectiveness and fairness of AI detection, and the assessment designs that hold up in an AI-rich environment. Following PRISMA 2020, seven databases and organisational sources were searched for studies published between January 2018 and June 2026. Thirty studies were included, eleven from Africa and four from Tanzania; they were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, AMSTAR 2 and the AACODS checklist and synthesised thematically with frequency counts. Five themes emerged: widespread and rising student use of GenAI (50% of studies); the vulnerability of conventional take-home and online assessment (60%); the unreliability and unfairness of AI-detection software (27%); the partial protection offered by authentic, process-focused and oral assessment (37%); and policy, capacity and training gaps (60%), most acute in African institutions. The evidence indicates that Tanzanian universities cannot rely on detection. They should move from a policing model to a design model of integrity, supported by institutional guidance, staff development and a graded scale of acceptable AI use. A Tanzanian Assessment Redesign Framework (TARF) is proposed for empirical testing, and priorities for intervention research are identified.

paper_title: From Aligned Embeddings to Instruction-Following Perception: A Survey of Vision–Language Model Development
paper_abstract: Recognizing an object from a text label, describing an unfamiliar scene, and following an instruction about a small image region require different forms of visual-language correspondence. The development of vision-language models can be understood through the effort to support these increasingly varied outputs. This survey follows the transition from contrastive image-text representations to captioning and grounding systems, and then to instruction-tuned multimodal language models. Within this account, we examine how pretraining objectives, web-data curation, visual connectors, and adaptation methods affect the tasks a model can perform. Particular attention is given to novel object captioning and dense prediction: both expose information that can be lost when image-level alignment is used as the starting point for a more specific task. Relative contrastive alignment [Fan et al., 2023] and uncertainty-guided cross-head co-training [Fan et al., 2022] offer complementary case studies of supervision quality. Evaluation and hallucination are considered alongside the capabilities they are meant to measure. The review brings together architectural comparisons, task-oriented evidence, and unresolved questions about visual resolution, grounding, and benchmark validity. Its central concern is how a system’s training signal and representation support the visual claims it ultimately makes.

paper_title: From Human Corrections to Learned Segmentations: A Critical Mathematical Review of Information, Learning, and Human Effort
paper_abstract: When does a human correction become useful learning, and what establishes better segmentation at matched human effort? This critical narrative review follows feedback through its selection, learner update, and evaluation. It compares active learning, machine teaching, interactive segmentation, and sequential predictive evaluation using a common mathematical account of target information, predictive error, response predictability, and human work. An exact Bayesian update converts evaluation-label information into expected log-loss improvement; an excess-risk decomposition explains what an approximate learner can lose. Conditional information decompositions separate the roles of selected locations, labels, and displayed context. Empirical comparisons show why response protocols, update mechanisms, and effort denominators matter, distinguishing current-mask refinement from reusable learning and simulated interaction from human evidence. We identify what logs can reveal, what requires independent evaluation, and what remains model-dependent. The resulting research priorities are to test what selection reveals, whether using it improves assimilation, and whether the resulting interaction policy benefits segmentation at matched effort. These are distinct claims: predicting a teacher's responses need not identify human intentions or establish better learning. No new acquisition algorithm or empirical superiority is claimed.
comments: 40 pages, literature-selection and search record included

paper_title: Can We Believe AI Peer Review?
paper_abstract: As large language models become widely used in scientific review and manuscript revision, AI scores are increasingly serving as feedback for assessing paper quality and guiding edits. Yet whether a single AI score reliably reflects the reviewer's judgment, and whether revision gains based on that score are endorsed by other reviewers, remain understudied. Using 200 papers from ICLR 2025 and 2026 and approximately 14,000 AI reviews, we study score reliability, score-distribution estimation, and cross-model agreement on revision gains. Repeated reviews fluctuate even under identical conditions. Finer-grained scoring protocols reduce score variance but also systematically shift mean scores, while the gains assigned to manuscript revisions depend strongly on the reviewer.

paper_title: Towards Adaptive and Real-Survey-Aligned Simulated Urban Mobility Behaviour of Generative Agents
paper_abstract: In existing agent-based simulations of multimodal urban mobility, agents, representing humans, choose their travel modes either using discrete choice or machine learning models fitted on structured travel survey data, or with rules explicitly written by the domain experts. Such approaches fix a priori the agents' possible behaviour space. Hence, a factor absent from variables or rules cannot affect agents' decisions. In reality, choosing a transport mode is a multidimensional decision in which objective and subjective factors intertwine and change over time. Integrating such complexity into a city-scale multimodal mobility simulation remains a challenge. Generative agents (GAs) built on large language models promise to respond to this challenge because they carry decision heuristics that travel surveys do not record. However, to the best of our knowledge, aligning their decisions with real household travel surveys remains an open question. In this paper, we build an agent-based model of daily multimodal mobility for Toulouse (France). We compare the performance of fifteen decision-makers (simple baselines, models fitted on the survey, GAs with minimal and tuned prompts, and a typed classifier) on the real household travel survey. Our results show that GAs with tuned prompts come close to the fitted models on the modal split of a simulated day without transport disruptions, but not trip by trip. GAs also react when unforeseen events occur. The recently released Jev-1.13 TypeSafe classifier gives surprisingly great results, showing that generating output text is not necessary. The results presented in this paper would be of interest to transport policy makers and service providers looking to apply generative agent-based modelling for improving urban mobility services.

paper_title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review
paper_abstract: Reviewer lottery error describes error due to a small set of peer reviews attending to only some of the issues with a paper that a larger pool of eligible reviewers would raise. We show this error can be reduced by surfacing a checklist of criticisms learned from a historical review corpus. Our approach generates a tree of checklists representing coarsenings of the atomic review claim space, then selects the coarsening that maximizes a theoretically-motivated measure of correlated agreement among reviewers. We realize this approach with an LLM-assisted pipeline and test it on NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022 review data. In simulated review with LLM reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of a three reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and on both venues the checklist with the highest correlated agreement has the lowest error for committees of three or more. In a human study with 20 participants, the learned NeurIPS checklist lowers the MSE of a paper ranking, measured against the NeurIPS 2021 order, from 0.48 to 0.22.
